title: Using hormones without a prescription
kicker: For trans and gender diverse people
intro: Some people take hormones they got without a prescription, for example online, from overseas or from a friend. This page is for you, and it is written without judgement. It covers ways to lower the risks, where to get clean needles in South Australia, and how to move to prescribed care when you are ready. It is general information, not medical advice.

body: This page is for adults who take, or are thinking about taking, gender-affirming hormones without a prescription. Some people call this DIY hormones.

People have many reasons. In a national survey of 928 trans Australians, a third said the path to getting hormones was too hard [14]. Some could not find a doctor to prescribe, or found the cost of doctor visits or scripts too high [14]. Others face long, complicated processes, worries about privacy, or being misgendered [15]. Many trans people say they avoid health care because they fear discrimination [2].
Whatever your reasons, you deserve safe care. The steps below can lower the risks while you work out what comes next.

sections.h: A prescription may be closer than you think
body: Most adults in Australia can start hormones with a GP. You do not usually need a letter from a psychiatrist. You make the decision, once your doctor has explained the benefits and risks [1, p12].
[Where to start with hormones](#/where-to-start) walks you through the first steps, one at a time.

sections.h: Hormones bought online or from overseas
body: Medicines bought online from overseas companies are not regulated by the TGA, Australia's medicines regulator. The TGA says you cannot tell if they are fake, toxic or contain illegal ingredients [7]. A product can have the wrong amount of hormone, or none at all [16].
Estradiol injections are made up specially (compounded) and are not approved by the TGA [1, p27].

To bring in a prescription medicine for yourself, you need a valid written Australian prescription. An e-script does not count, and you can bring in no more than 3 months' supply at a time [4]. Known fake medicines are taken at the border, even if you have a prescription [4]. Other packages without the right papers can be taken and destroyed, and you lose your money [5].
Testosterone needs an import permit [6]. The TGA says controlled substances cannot be brought in under its personal import scheme [5].
The TGA says it is illegal to give or sell medicines you bought online to people outside your family [8].
list: Keep the box, or take a photo of the label, so a doctor or pharmacist can see what you take
Write down what you take, how much and when
Do not use a product if the seal is broken, or if oil looks cloudy or has bits in it

body: Taking more does not always work better, and higher doses can bring more risk [1, p27]. These are the main risks to know about.
list: **Estradiol and blood clots:** in studies of cisgender women, estradiol tablets raise the risk of clots, and patches and gel do not [1, p26]. Estradiol injections carry a similar risk to tablets [1, p26]. The risk is highest in the first year [2]. It is also higher if you smoke, are above a healthy weight or are over 45 [1, p26].
**Ethinylestradiol:** this is a different form of oestrogen with the highest clot risk, so it is best avoided [2].
**Estradiol injections:** they can push blood levels well above the target range, so low starting doses are advised [1, p27].

**Cyproterone:** a low dose lowers testosterone as well as a higher dose, with fewer side effects [1, p27]. The Australian product information reports meningioma (a growth in the lining of the brain) with long-term use at 25 mg a day and above [3]. High doses add to this risk [1, p27].
**Spironolactone:** it can raise potassium in the blood if your kidneys do not work well, or if you take some heart or blood pressure medicines. This is very uncommon in healthy people [1, p27].
**Testosterone:** it thickens the blood [1, p24]. If haematocrit (the share of the blood that is red cells) goes above 0.5, doctors look at lowering the dose [2].
**Testosterone and pregnancy:** testosterone is not contraception, and it can harm a pregnancy. Use contraception if you could get pregnant [1, p22].
**Your liver:** the body clears estradiol less well if your liver is not working well [2].
after: [Doses and formulations](#/doses) shows the doses that Australian prescribers use.

sections.h: Blood tests can show how your body is going
body: Blood tests show your hormone levels and whether your body is coping. Routine tests may include a full blood count, kidney function and electrolytes, liver function, and hormone levels [1, p36].
A GP can order these tests. You can ask for them even before you have a prescription.
after: [Blood tests](#/monitoring) explains the tests for each medicine and what the results mean.

body: If you inject hormones, these steps lower the risk of infection and injury.
list: Never share needles, syringes or vials, even with a partner. Shared equipment can spread HIV and hepatitis C [9][12]
Ask a doctor or nurse to show you how. Testosterone injections are given by a doctor, or by you or a friend who has been shown how [22]
Use a new needle and syringe each time, and rotate your sites: see [Injecting testosterone at home](#/using/injecting-at-home)
Ask for the needle and syringe sizes that suit you, and write them down
after: [Injecting testosterone at home](#/using/injecting-at-home) has the full steps, with pictures, and the signs that need a check the same day.

sections.h: Where to get clean needles and syringes
body: South Australia's Needle and Syringe Program (it used to be called the Clean Needle Program) gives out sterile needles and syringes, sharps containers, information and referral [9]. Drug and Alcohol Services South Australia (DASSA) runs it [9].
SA Health counts people who use steroids and other people who inject for health reasons among the many people who use needles [13].
list: **Program sites:** there are sites across Adelaide and country South Australia, including several Aboriginal community controlled health services. Find your nearest on the [SA Health site list](https://www.sahealth.sa.gov.au/wps/wcm/connect/public+content/sa+health+internet/resources/dassa+nsp+list+by+region) [10].
**At any time:** some sites have a 24-hour syringe vending machine, including some country hospitals [10].

**Hepatitis SA:** peer-run sites at Hackney, Noarlunga, Port Adelaide and Elizabeth give free needles and syringes in office hours. Hepatitis SA also lists free 24-hour machines at Hackney, Elizabeth, Hendon, Noarlunga and Stepney [11].
**Pharmacies:** participating pharmacies across Adelaide and country South Australia sell sterile needle packs, and take back used sharps [12].
**Not sure where to go?** Call the Alcohol and Drug Information Service (ADIS) on 1300 131 340 [9].
after: Ask staff for the needle and syringe sizes you were taught to use. Sites do not all stock the same range of equipment [10], so call first to check they have your sizes.
Outside South Australia, the [AIVL national NSP directory](https://aivl.org.au/nsp-directory/) finds sites near you by postcode or suburb [21].

sections.h: Getting rid of used needles safely
body: Put used needles and syringes straight into a sharps container or another rigid-walled container. Take it to a Needle and Syringe Program site, or to a pharmacy with a sharps bin [13]. Program sites give out sharps containers with their equipment [13].
Call the Alcohol and Drug Information Service on 1300 131 340 to find your nearest sharps disposal point [13].
If someone else is pricked by a used needle, they should let it bleed, wash it with soap and water, and cover it. Then they should get medical advice straight away [23].
after: [Disposing of needles and leftover medicine](#/using#sec-using-11) has the full steps.

body: Call 000 for an ambulance straight away if you have:
list: Sudden or worse breathlessness, chest pain, a racing heart, coughing up blood, or fainting. These can be signs of a clot in the lung [19]
A drooping face or mouth, weak arms, or slurred speech. These can be signs of a stroke [20]
after: Pain, redness and swelling in your calf or thigh can be a clot in the leg (DVT). See a doctor straight away [18]. Call 000 if you also become short of breath, have chest pain or feel dizzy or faint [18].
If you have taken too much of a medicine, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 [9]. For other health worries, call healthdirect on 1800 022 222 [19].

sections.h: Talking to a doctor or pharmacist
body: It is OK to tell a GP or pharmacist what you take. Australia's standards of care tell GPs to ask about hormones you have taken before, prescribed or otherwise [1, p19]. Knowing helps them keep you safe.
Bring the box or a photo of the label, and say how much you take and how often.

Your health information is protected by privacy law. A doctor or pharmacist can only share it in some situations, such as when you agree, when the law requires it, or to prevent a serious threat to someone's life or health [17].
If a doctor is not supportive, you can see another one. [If a GP says no, or is not sure](#/where-to-start#sec-where-to-start-5) has ideas.

sections.h: Moving to prescribed care, and what it costs
body: You can move to prescribed hormones at any time. With a prescription, your medicine comes from an Australian pharmacy, and your doctor goes through your blood tests with you.
Testosterone on the PBS needs an Authority script. Short-acting testosterone injections are not on the PBS, so you pay the full private price [1, p33].
[Costs and the PBS](#/costs) shows what each medicine costs and how to pay less. If cost is stopping you, see [If cost is a barrier](#/costs#sec-costs-11).
